Non-Profit Community Support Services Program (CDBG-DR) Request for Applications: Mental Health 1 | Page 1.0 INTRODUCTION The City of St. Petersburg (the City) is issuing a competitive Request for Applications (RFA) to award U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) Community Development Block Grant–Disaster Recovery (CDBG‑DR) funds through the City's Non‑Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) Program. The NPCSS Program (also referred to as ‘the Program’) is built to strengthen the community by helping nonprofits offer the care and support people need after disaster, so residents can recover and prepare for the future. This RFA, the first in a series of funding opportunities under the NPCSS Program, is specifically focused on identifying subrecipients who will provide mental health and wraparound support services as described in this document. This is not a grantmaking opportunity where organizations apply to meet their individual needs; this is a solicitation where the City is procuring a specific set of services to meet the needs of city residents. EXPLANATION: Congress appropriated funds through the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) Community Development Block Grant - Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) Program in response to the 2023 Hurricane Idalia (DR-4734-FL) and the 2024 Hurricane Helene (DR-4828- FL). Assistance for these disasters was appropriated on December 21, 2024, by the Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act of 2025. The City of St. Petersburg (City) was allocated $159,884,000 per the Allocation Announcement Notice (90 FR 4759) published on January 16, 2025. On June 12, 2025, City Council approved the CDBG-DR Action Plan for the use of the federal grant funds (Resolution No. 2025-327) which allocated $6,000,000 to the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program. HUD approved the City’s Action Plan in August 2025 and executed the City’s Grant Agreement in February 2026. Through extensive public input and Unmet Needs and Mitigation Needs Assessments in the Action Plan, the City determined the need to create the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program to address the increased need for essential community services as a result of the qualifying disasters. This is the funding available for all three core services combined, meaning each selected organization will receive an award below this maximum amount. Outlined below are the award caps for each Core Service type: • Case Management award: up to $725,000 • Assertive Outreach award: up to $175,000 • Clinical Mental Health Services award: up to $350,000 Each organization must submit a budget that does not exceed the maximum award cap for the Core Service type(s) for which they are applying. If an organization is applying to administer multiple Core Services, the submitted budget must not exceed the combined total of both Core Service award caps. For example, if an organization applies for Case Management and Assertive Outreach, the budget cannot exceed $900,000. In this scenario, the organization must still break out the budget into sections outlining which costs are related to Case Management and which costs are related to Assertive Outreach. items.title: 04 | MANAGEMENT, OPERATIONS, + GOVERNANCE TRAILS CROSSING MASTER PLAN 103102 CONCEPTUAL REVENUE ANALYSIS Achieving full ﬁ nancial self-sustainability at Trails Crossing will be challenging. While the City may play a role in supporting capital improvements, grants, and other funding opportunities, the extent of that participation has not yet been established. A comprehensive and diversiﬁ ed ﬁ nancial strategy will therefore be needed to supplement earned revenue and support long-term operations and maintenance. ENTERPRISE MODEL VIABILITY AND REVENUE DIVERSITY At the St. Petersburg Pier, the enterprise facility generates signiﬁ cant annual revenue – approximately $1.5 million – through tenant leases and events. However, even with this substantial income, the Pier still relies on city subsidies for the remainder of its funding. Because of the unique constraints of Trails Crossing, an enterprise funding model – whereby the cultural linear park would operate like a self-sustaining private business – is currently not recommended. A healthy balance of leases, events, sponsorships, and city support is key to ensuring ﬁ nancial stability and resilience, particularly during disruptions. PHIL

items.title: 100 City of St. Petersburg | Moffatt & Nichol FINAL DRAFT SPARKMAN WHARF – TAMPA, FLORIDA Sparkman Wharf is a dynamic waterfront development that blends a working port with a vibrant mix of retail, dining, and entertainment options. It stands as a prime example of a successful working waterfront that serves both economic and recreational needs. WHERE Sparkman Wharf is located on the site of the formerly under performing Channelside Bay Plaza, part of the Water Street Tampa project. It sits along the Garrison Channel in downtown Tampa. WHAT Sparkman Wharf revitalizes a previously underutilized waterfront area, combining a working port with retail, dining, and entertainment options. The project is named after Stephen Sparkman, Tampa’s first congressman, known for his efforts in securing federal funding for Port Tampa Bay. Developed through a partnership between Tampa Bay Lightning owner Jeff Vinik and Bill Gates’ Cascade Investment, Sparkman Wharf replaced the failed Channelside Bay Plaza. The development includes a one-acre event lawn, a biergarten, a dining garden, and waterfront loft-style office spaces. Year-round programming of live music and events accommodates up to 500 people

items.title: Section 5. Authority to Underfill Positions. Notwithstanding Section 10-1 of the City Code, the City Manager, or designee, will have the authority to fill an authorized position with a position in a lower classification to provide flexibility for the recruitment of personnel, and the training required to bring an employee to the minimum requirements of the higher classification that is an authorized position. Section 6. Budget Transfer Procedures. Section 5.05 of the City Charter authorizes the City Manager to transfer unencumbered appropriations within departments and funds. Transfers from one department to another and transfers from one fund to another shall be approved by City Commission. The C ity Manager may also create accounts needed for proper budgeting purposes, provided that the funds for that account are appropriated through budget transfers in accordance with Section 5.05 of the City’s Charter and Section 6 of this Ordinance. items.title: Please accept this letter as my strong and enthusiastic endorsement of the Early Learning Coalition (ELC) of Broward County’s grant application to the City of Sunrise. At Broward College, we witness firsthand the life-changing impact of the School Readiness program. For many of our student-parents, access to affordable, high-quality childcare is not merely a support service, it is the deciding factor in whether they can persist, complete their degrees, and transition successfully into the workforce. By alleviating this critical financial burden, ELC Broward empowers parents with stability and peace of mind, enabling them to fully invest in their education and career advancement. The City of Sunrise’s investment in this initiative yields far-reaching benefits beyond individual families. It strengthens the local economy by supporting small childcare businesses and sustaining the educators who serve our youngest learners. At the same time, it ensures that children enter school socially and academically prepared laying the foundation for long-term success that benefits the entire community. ELC Broward is a cornerstone of economic mobility and educational equity in our region. I strong

Mr. Power described the alternatives evaluated and discussed with residents in March, including roadway changes, additional drains, property acquisition, retention areas, and relocation of the pump station. He explained that a substantial retention solution would require approximately three to four acres and that no suitable commercial property owner had agreed to sell. He also reviewed ongoing efforts to identify additional drain locations, improve the Little Harbor outfall, clean drainage systems, and enforce private property maintenance obligations throughout the City. Mr. Power outlined the revised emergency response procedures, including monitoring rainfall and tides, preparing trucks and pumps for immediate deployment, placing crews on standby, checking inlets, and cleaning drainage systems after rain events. He stated that the City had obtained access through a mobile home park to route temporary pumping equipment to a Federal Highway drainage inlet that discharges to another location. The Haven on Vine redevelopment project requires new firewater main infrastructure to provide fire protection services to the property and support the required fire sprinkler systems. Cathcart Construction Company – Florida, LLC provided preliminary budgetary pricing of $715,400 for the proposed installation. The final scope and pricing will be subject to completed engineering plans, permitting, and negotiations. A 15% contingency ($107,310) is requested to address unforeseen field conditions and necessary changes, resulting in a total not-to-exceed authorization of $822,710.

The City will fund the project through its State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) funds. The City will execute and record a mortgage lien and corresponding promissory note in the amount of $242,680.70 against the property to secure the financial assistance. The mortgage and promissory note will establish a 30-year affordability period commencing on the date the documents are executed. Consistent with the City's Local Housing Assistance Plan (LHAP) and applicable program guidelines, the assistance will be structured as a deferred, forgivable loan with a 30-year term. The loan will be forgiven at the conclusion of the affordability period, provided the homeowner has remained in compliance with all applicable loan terms and conditions and has not defaulted. Should the final project costs exceed the currently approved amount of $242,680.70, the mortgage and promissory note may be amended to reflect the additional costs, provided the total assistance does not exceed the $350,000 maximum assistance amount established in the City's LHAP.

SUMMARY: On November 18, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners (BCC) approved the annual roofing services contracts (R2025-1661 through R2025-1663). The work consists of repair and replacement of existing roofing for County owned and leased buildings on an as-needed basis. The contractors now join the list of 14 prequalified contractors for a total of 16 prequalified contractors with a contract expiration date of November 17, 2030. The specific requirements of the work will be determined by individual work orders issued against this annual roofing services contract. These contracts have a maximum cumulative value of $10,000,000 across all prequalified contractors. Work will be awarded as work orders on a lump-sum, competitively bid basis across all prequalified contractors. Contractors may qualify at any time and be added to this annual roofing services contract before the term ends. Projects less than $150,000 are bid among the pool of prequalified contractors. SUMMARY: On February 3, 2026, the Board of County Commissioners (BCC) directed staff to continue negotiations with Related Ross, LLC (Related) on a second hotel to support and complement the Palm Beach County Convention Center (Convention Center). SUMMARY: On March 10, 2026, the Village adopted an ordinance annexing approximately 446.14 acres of land, known as Artistry Lakes. The County objected to the annexation because the annexation area does not meet the requirements of Section 171.043, Florida Statutes. On March 26, 2026, the County passed a resolution initiating the Conflict Resolution Procedures under Chapter 164. Florida Statutes. On February 10, 2026, after discussions with the County, the Village initiated the Interlocal Service Boundary Agreement (ISBA) process to negotiate the terms under which the subject property and adjacent properties will be annexed. The County adopted its responding resolution on February 26, 2026. While the Village approved the ISBA, the Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners (BCC) denied it on August 26, 2026. On September 30th, 2026 the County Administrator and the Village Manager met per Ch. 164 Conflict Resolution Proceedings. Both the County Administrator and the Village Manager agreed to bring the ILA to their respective governing bodies. The County also agreed to bring the PBA to the BCC at the same time as the ILA. The Village Council approved the ILA on October 13, 2026.

Staff recommends motion to approve: the Annual Certified Budget for Arthropod Control (Form 13617) with the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS) for Mosquito Control activities performed during the Fiscal Year (FY) period beginning October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027. SUMMARY: As part of the FDACS routine agency review of Florida mosquito control programs participating in the “State Approved” mosquito control program, FDACS requests financial information from the mosquito control programs participating to determine what, if any, grant funding is allocated to each mosquito control program. As the total State grant is a finite amount, and is divided amongst the programs based on the tier they fall under, as determined by FDACS Form 13617, it is necessary that the County provide this financial report in order to maintain its participation in the “State Approved” mosquito control program. Since the Palm Beach County Mosquito Control Division’s budget exceeds $3M, it places the program in the State’s Tier I, which does not qualify for additional funding under Florida Administrative Code (F.A.C) 5E-13. There is no cost to the County. Countywide (FXM)
